title: Troy VI: the Citadel of the Poem

layers.note: The west wall, from the point in the north-west where the circuit simply stops to the West Gate VI U. This is the rougher, older work of the ring — unwrought stone, where the south and east stretches are cut ashlar — and Dörpfeld took those finer stretches for a rebuilding within the life of Troy VI, which is why the circuit reads as two buildings joined. The line is a polygon and not a curve: “im Äusseren sehen wir die Linie der Mauer als Polygon aus geraden Stücken von fast gleicher Länge gebildet” (Dörpfeld 1902, 2:611) — straight lengths of nearly equal size, each set a little forward of the last, so the wall turns the hill in steps and never has to make a corner, a corner being the weak point of a defense. Every offset drawn here is one he surveyed. House VI A stands hard against the inner face along this stretch and is drawn with the wall, because it is drawn with the wall on his plate. Traced from Dörpfeld's Tafel V, rectified on the plate's own 20 m grid; every vertex is his linework, not a smoothing of it.

layers.note: The south wall, from the West Gate VI U to the South Gate VI T, ending in the south tower VI i. Measured across the drawn band the masonry runs 4.4 to 5.3 m thick along here. Dörpfeld printed the wall in two tones and said why: “bei der Festungsmauer ist der Unterbau hellrot, die dünnere Obermauer dunkelrot getönt” (1902, 2:650) — the substructure light red, the thinner upper wall dark red. This plate draws the two together, as one footprint, because that is what a reader standing outside the wall would have seen: one face. Homer's Trojans have their wall from a god. Poseidon made it πόλιν πέρι τεῖχος ... εὐρύ τε καὶ μάλα καλόν, wide and very beautiful, that the city might be unbreakable (Il. 21.446-47), and resents that men will remember the Achaeans' wall and forget the one he and Apollo built for Laomedon (7.452-53). This ring is what Hector runs. Achilles drives him past the lookout and the windy fig tree, out from under the wall along the wagon-track — παρὰ σκοπιὴν καὶ ἐρινεὸν ἠνεμόεντα / τείχεος αἰὲν ὑπ’ ἐκ κατ’ ἀμαξιτὸν ἐσσεύοντο (Il. 22.145-46) — and three times they wheel round Priam’s city, τρὶς Πριάμοιο πόλιν πέρι δινηθήτην, with all the gods looking on (22.165-66). Measured round the outside of this circuit, off the plan, the lap is about 535 m. Three of them come to a mile, almost exactly. Homer never says the wall is long. He says it is unbreakable, and lets the two of them run. Traced from Dörpfeld's Tafel V, rectified on the plate's own 20 m grid; every vertex is his linework, not a smoothing of it. How the sheet was made: Tafel V, drawn at 1:800, was rectified on its own printed 20 m grid — ninety-nine grid intersections recovered by line-fitting, a projective transform fitted through them, mean residual 0.15 m of ground and worst 0.5 m, finer than the drawn line itself. The squares check against Dörpfeld's own text: the shaft wells he places in J 4 and K 4 fall in squares J 4 and K 4 here. Everything on this sheet is therefore his survey at one uniform scale, 218 m of ground east to west by 200 m north to south — the sheet is carried north beyond the last surveyed stone so that the whole ring stands on it. It is oriented as he printed it — “der Plan ist nach der magnetischen Nordlinie orientirt”, to the magnetic north line of the 1890s and not to true north — and no rotation has been applied. The modern excavation net kept his 20 m grid and tied it to a world coordinate system by GPS in 2000 (Messmer 2014), so this plan can be put on the ground; the plate does not do it, because a citadel plan wants the wall, not a latitude.

layers.note: The south-east and east wall, from the South Gate VI T to the East Gate VI S, with the great tower VI h jutting from it. This is the finest masonry on the site: rectangular limestone laid without mortar, the face battered so that it leans back as it rises, and stepped forward every few meters in the offsets this trace keeps. The tower stands midway between the two gates — “der Turm VI h liegt in der Mitte zwischen den zwei Thoren VI S und VI T” (Dörpfeld 1902, 1:121 ff.) — which is where a tower belongs, at the point where the wall face has to be swept from the flank. Traced from Dörpfeld's Tafel V, rectified on the plate's own 20 m grid; every vertex is his linework, not a smoothing of it.

layers.note: The north-east stretch: the outer arm of the East Gate, run out beyond the circuit and overlapping it, and the wall running north from it toward the great tower. The overlap is the most sophisticated piece of military architecture on the hill. It turns the approach to the East Gate into a blind corridor, so that the door cannot be seen from outside and cannot be come at head-on — a ram cannot be brought to a gate it cannot see. Traced from Dörpfeld's Tafel V, rectified on the plate's own 20 m grid; every vertex is his linework, not a smoothing of it.

layers.label: Restored after Dörpfeld
layers.note: The north wall — restored, not surveyed. Not a stone of it has ever been seen: everything on this side was cut away for the precinct of Athena long before a spade came. Dörpfeld would not put it on his survey plan. “Den ganzen nördlichen und nordwestlichen Teil der Burgmauer, von dem keine Spur erhalten ist, habe ich deshalb auch nicht einmal durch punktirte Linien anzudeuten gewagt” (1902, 2:650) — of the whole northern and north-western part of the citadel wall, of which no trace survives, he did not dare even to suggest the line with dots. He did restore it elsewhere, on his own conjectural plan at Fig. 470, “Ergänzter Plan der Burg Troja mit Umgebung” (1902, 2:610), and it is that restoration, his and nobody else’s, that is drawn here. It is drawn hollow — the two faces of a wall at the width of the surveyed masonry it continues, with the interior left open and lightly hatched — where every surveyed stretch on this sheet is a filled band of stone. The width is a drawing convention and not a measurement: nobody has measured the thickness of a wall nobody has seen, and matching the band beside it is what says this wall, here, restored. What the line carries is the course, at the excavator’s hand. No offsets, no gate: those exist for the south and the east because somebody measured them, and they do not exist here. How the line got onto this sheet:  the circuit of Fig. 470 was lifted off the page image as a centreline and fitted to the surveyed trace by a plane similarity — scale and shift only, no rotation, since both drawings are his and both are printed to the same magnetic north line. Across the 497 vertices of the surviving circuit the fit stands at a mean of 3.3 m, finer than the width of the line on his small figure; a free fit put the rotation at 6° and did not improve on that, so none was applied. The drawn stretch runs between the two points where the survey stops, and each end is eased onto the broken wall face it meets — 1.5 m of correction at the west wall, 3.9 m at the great tower, both inside the fit’s own error. The raster centreline was resampled at about 3 m and lightly smoothed, which takes out the scan’s own jitter and nothing else. No other adjustment was made, and one place shows what that costs: near the tower the restored line runs across VI R, the fragment Dörpfeld locates outside the wall’s line. His survey plan and his restored plan disagree there by about 3 m, and the disagreement is left standing rather than tidied away. A line lifted off a 1902 vignette is good to a few meters and no better, and that is the measure of what this stretch of Troy is known to. The poem needs this side of the city and cannot have it. The Scaean Gate opens πεδίον δέ, out toward the plain and the ships, and no gate on the surveyed circuit faces that way: there was a gate along here. Dörpfeld set it at the north-west corner vermutungsweise, by conjecture, and admitted in the same breath that it “auch weiter östlich gelegen haben kann”, that it might equally have lain further east (1902, 2:610). No point is marked for it on this plate, because there is no coordinate to mark. This is also the stretch Andromache knows is weak. She tells Hector to post the army παρ’ ἐρινεόν, by the fig tree, ἔνθα μάλιστα / ἀμβατός ἐστι πόλις καὶ ἐπίδρομον ἔπλετο τεῖχος — where the city is most open to assault and the wall can be climbed (Il. 6.433-34); three times the best of the Achaeans have come and tried it there already, τρὶς γὰρ τῇ γ’ ἐλθόντες ἐπειρήσανθ’ οἱ ἄριστοι (6.435). Dörpfeld letters ERINEOS-HUEGEL on Fig. 470 on the ground just west of this lost arc, an identification that is his and not the poem’s. The one length of wall the Iliad calls climbable is the one length the spade cannot show.

layers.note: Tower VI g, the largest on the circuit, drawn with the surviving north-east end of the wall that carries it. Tolman and Scoggin, following Dörpfeld, give it 18 m broad and projecting 8 m, “the most stately tower”; inside it a shaft sunk to water gave the citadel its supply under cover. North of this the circuit stops. Dörpfeld notes independently that a shaft well of Troy VI, his B b, lies in square K 4 — which is this tower. The poem has a great tower too, and does not say which. Andromache is not at home when Hector comes for her: ἀλλ’ ἐπὶ πύργον ἔβη μέγαν Ἰλίου — she had gone up to the great tower of Ilios, having heard the Trojans were breaking (Il. 6.386). At the end Hector waits for Achilles πύργῳ ἔπι προὔχοντι φαεινὴν ἀσπίδ’ ἐρείσας — his bright shield leaned against the tower that juts out (22.97). Nothing on this plan is identified with either. The poem’s towers carry no letters, and the letters carry no verses. Traced from Dörpfeld's Tafel V, rectified on the plate's own 20 m grid; every vertex is his linework, not a smoothing of it.

layers.note: House VI M, about 29 by 21 m over all — the largest single building left standing inside the circuit — set on its own terrace above the south wall, with open ground between it and the ring. Homer gives Priam a palace of polished stone with fifty chambers for his sons and twelve more across the court for his daughters' husbands (Il. 6.242-50). The largest hall the spade has found inside this wall would stand inside one wing of that. Traced from Dörpfeld's Tafel V, rectified on the plate's own 20 m grid; every vertex is his linework, not a smoothing of it.

layers.note: The block of the east terrace — Dörpfeld's houses VI D, VI C, VI E and VI F, drawn together because they are drawn together, wall against wall, on his sheet. VI C is the hall in the middle of the block. The citadel was built as terraces rising toward the center, each held up by a retaining wall with the houses standing on the level ground behind, and this is the second of them. The double circles Dörpfeld draws inside these rooms are pithoi, storage jars sunk in the floors (1902, 2:649). layers.label: Gate VI U
layers.note: The West Gate, VI U, with an opening about 2.50 m across (Tolman and Scoggin 1903). During the life of Troy VI it was walled up: Dörpfeld draws the blocking across the passage in hatching, so the defenders closed their own gate — the sort of fact a plan records and a poem does not. Nothing is drawn here but the name. A gate is a gap in the masonry, and masonry is what this plate traces.

layers.label: Gate VI T
layers.note: The South Gate, VI T — 3.20 to 3.35 m broad, its roadway paved and carrying a drainage channel half a meter deep and 0.30 to 0.40 m wide (Tolman and Scoggin 1903), flanked by tower VI i. Dörpfeld took it for the main gate: “das Hauptthor der VI. Burg ist wahrscheinlich das Süd-Thor VI T gewesen”, and identified it with Homer's Dardanian Gates, on the reasoning that Dardania lay toward Ida in the south-east — “ich ohne Zögern das Thor VI T als das dardanische bezeichnet ... habe” (1902, 2:630). The identification is his reading of the poem against the ground, not a find: no gate at Hisarlık has been shown to be a gate Homer names. Hector keeps breaking for the Dardanian Gates during the chase, hoping to get in under the well-built towers (Il. 22.194-95).

layers.label: Gate VI S
layers.note: The East Gate, VI S — a passage about 2 m wide and a door only about 1.80 m broad (Tolman and Scoggin 1903), reached along the corridor between the wall and the outer arm drawn beside it, with steps and a ramp carrying the way up inside. Dörpfeld sections it at his Fig. 41, “das Ost-Thor in der VI. Schicht (VI S) und in der VII. Schicht (VII S)”. He allowed that Homer's Scaean Gate “kann ... weiter östlich gelegen haben und würde dann vielleicht mit dem Nordost-Thor zusammenfallen” (1902, 2:630) — might have lain further east and coincided with the north-east gate. Allowed, not shown.

layers.label: Pergamos
layers.note: The summit — and an absence, not a find. Homer's Pergamos is the top of the citadel. Apollo's temple stands Περγάμῳ εἰν ἱερῇ (Il. 5.446); he and Ares look down from it on the fighting (4.508, 7.21); Paris comes striding down from Περγάμου ἄκρης (6.512); Cassandra climbs it and is the first to see Hector's body coming home (24.700). The temple of Athena ἐν πόλει ἄκρῃ that the Trojan women go up to with the robe belongs here (6.88, 6.297), and so do the houses of Priam and of Hector (6.317). Of all of it there is nothing to plan: the Hellenistic and Roman levelling for the precinct of Athena of Ilion cut the top off the mound and took Troy VI's summit with it. The part of Troy the Iliad names most often is the part the excavation cannot reach. No outline is drawn here, only the name, over the ground where it stood.

layers.note: The outer of the two lines Dörpfeld ruled inside the citadel on his restored plan (Fig. 470), standing back from the wall face by seven to thirteen meters all round. He gives them no key, and the plan of the ground says what they are: the citadel was built as terraces rising toward the center, each held up by a retaining wall with the houses standing on the level behind it, and this is the front of the first of them. What lies between it and the masonry is the ring street — “im Innern finden wir eine breite Ringstrasse, mehrere zum Centrum der Burg gerichtete Querstrassen” (1902, 2:611), a broad ring street with several cross streets running in toward the center — the circulation that lets defenders reach any stretch of the circuit without crossing built-up ground. He drew the line dotted, which on his sheets means restored: the terrace fronts went with everything else above the courses that survived. The east terrace houses stand across it here because they stand across it on his own plate. Lifted from Fig. 470 by the same plane similarity that carries the restored north circuit onto this sheet — scale and shift only, no rotation — and drawn in the same open register at a lighter weight, because it is the same kind of claim: the excavator’s line, not the excavator’s measurement. This is the ring Homer’s Trojans keep running: the women go up through the city to the temple ἐν πόλει ἄκρῃ (Il. 6.297), and Hector comes down from it to the Scaean Gate by the way everyone in the poem uses and nobody in the poem describes.

layers.note: The inner line of Fig. 470: the front of the highest terrace Dörpfeld would draw at all, ringing the top of the mound. Inside it is Pergamos, and inside it there is nothing to plan — the Hellenistic and Roman levelling for the precinct of Athena of Ilion cut the summit off and took Troy VI’s topmost terrace with it, which is why this line is the last thing on the sheet before the name. Restored, after Fig. 470, on the same fit as the north circuit and drawn in the same open register: not a course of it was measured. What stood within it is the part of the city the Iliad names most — Apollo’s temple Περγάμῳ εἰν ἱερῇ (5.446), the houses of Priam and of Hector (6.317), the roof Paris comes striding down from (6.512) — and the part the excavation cannot reach.

layers.label: House of Priam
layers.note: The house of Priam, where the poem puts it and where nobody has dug. Hector comes to it Πριάμοιο δόμον περικαλλέ’ ... ξεστῇς αἰθούσῃσι τετυγμένον, the beautiful house built with polished colonnades; inside were fifty chambers of polished stone built close to one another, where Priam’s sons slept beside their wives, and across the court, facing them, twelve roofed chambers for the husbands of his daughters (Il. 6.242-50). That is a court with a range of building on either side, and it is drawn here as that and no more: the outer line is the wall of the αὐλή, the inner one the open court within it. Sixty-two chambers is a larger house than anything the spade has found inside this circuit — House VI M, the biggest, is about 29 by 21 m and would stand inside one wing of it. The position is the poem’s: the houses of Priam, Hector and Paris are ἐν πόλει ἄκρῃ, on the city height (6.317), and the height is the ground the Athena precinct later cut away. No stone of any of it has been seen. Size and shape are drawn to the poem’s own description; the point on the sheet is not a coordinate.

layers.label: The assembly
layers.note: The assembly ground, at Priam’s doors. When Iris comes to Troy with Zeus’s message she finds the Trojans in session: οἳ δ’ ἀγορὰς ἀγόρευον ἐπὶ Πριάμοιο θύρῃσι / πάντες ὁμηγερέες ἠμὲν νέοι ἠδὲ γέροντες — all gathered, young and old, holding assembly at Priam’s doors (Il. 2.788-89). The poem gives the assembly no building and no walls, only a place: outside the palace door. It is drawn as open ground against the palace’s south front, which is the whole of what the line supports.

layers.label: House of Hector
layers.note: The house of Hector, named with the other two on the height: Paris built his own δώματα ἐγγύθι τε Πριάμοιο καὶ Ἕκτορος ἐν πόλει ἄκρῃ, near Priam’s and Hector’s, on the city height (Il. 6.316-17). This is the house Hector comes to and does not find Andromache in — she has gone up to the great tower — and the house he leaves for the last time by the same road down through the well-built streets (6.390-91). Drawn beside Priam’s because the poem says beside; the size is a house’s, not a measurement.

layers.label: House of Paris
layers.note: The house of Paris, the one building in Troy whose making the poem describes. He built it himself, καλά, τά ῥ’ αὐτὸς ἔτευξε σὺν ἀνδράσιν οἳ τότ’ ἄριστοι / ἦσαν ἐνὶ Τροίῃ ... τέκτονες ἄνδρες — with the men who were then the best builders in Troy — and they made him θάλαμον καὶ δῶμα καὶ αὐλήν, a chamber and a hall and a court, near Priam’s house and Hector’s, on the city height (Il. 6.313-17). Chamber, hall and court is a megaron with a yard, which is also the plan of every house Dörpfeld dug inside this wall; that agreement is worth noting and is not evidence of position.

layers.label: Temple of Athena
layers.note: The temple of Athena, ἐν πόλει ἄκρῃ. Hecuba takes the largest and most beautiful robe from her store and carries it up with the Trojan women: αἳ δ’ ὅτε νηὸν ἵκανον Ἀθήνης ἐν πόλει ἄκρῃ, and Theano, whom the Trojans had made Athena’s priestess, opened the doors to them (Il. 6.297-300). The poem locates it on the height and says nothing of its size or plan. What stood on this ground in historical times was the precinct of Athena of Ilion — and the levelling for it is what destroyed the Bronze-Age summit, so that the one building the Iliad puts here is the one the excavation can never test.

layers.label: Shrine of Apollo
layers.note: The shrine of Apollo in Pergamos. Apollo carries Aeneas out of the fighting and sets him down Περγάμῳ εἰν ἱερῇ, ὅθι οἱ νηός γε τέτυκτο — in holy Pergamos, where his own temple was built — and Leto and Artemis heal him ἐν μεγάλῳ ἀδύτῳ, in the great inner chamber (Il. 5.446-48). Hector swears to hang the armor of the man he kills πρὸτι νηὸν Ἀπόλλωνος ἑκάτοιο, at the temple of far-shooting Apollo (7.83). An ἄδυτον called great is the only dimension the poem gives, and it is not one; the outline here is a shrine’s, set on the height with the rest.

layers.note: A street from the assembly ground down to the South Gate. Hector goes out of the house τὴν αὐτὴν ὁδὸν αὖτις ἐϋκτιμένας κατ’ ἀγυιάς — back by the same road, down the well-built streets — and εὖτε πύλας ἵκανε διερχόμενος μέγα ἄστυ, and when he reached the gates, having come through the great city (Il. 6.391-92). The poem is explicit that there is a made street from the houses on the height to the gate and that Hector uses it twice; it names no course. The line drawn here follows the citadel's own logic instead: it runs radially, crossing both of Dörpfeld’s terrace fronts and the ring street between them, which is what his own “mehrere zum Centrum der Burg gerichtete Querstrassen” (1902, 2:611) — several cross streets directed toward the center of the citadel — describes. Where it meets surveyed masonry it passes behind it.

layers.note: A second street, from the palace down to the West Gate VI U, on the same reasoning as the way to the south gate: a radial cross street cutting the terraces, the pattern Dörpfeld describes inside the wall. No third street is drawn to the East Gate VI S, and the absence is the honest result rather than an oversight — the ground between the height and that gate is the built-up terrace quarter, house against house on Dörpfeld's own plate, and the approach to VI S is the blind corridor between the wall and its outer arm. There is no line to draw there that would not run through excavated buildings.
